claim_decisions.statement: The 2023 study reports drought–IPV associations, not causation. Precipitation analysis used 122,696 married women across NFHS 2015–16 and 2019–21; government-declared socioeconomic drought analysis used 62,464 women in NFHS 2015–16 only. Adjusted odds ratios vary by drought definition and violence type.
claim_decisions.uncertainty: Repeated cross-sectional design, self-reported violence and district drought classification limit inference. Household-income/consumption mediation was not tested; odds ratios are not changes in prevalence or individual risk.
claim_decisions.locator: Methods: Data and Analysis; Results Table 2; Discussion limitations

gaps: No complete causal income-mediated drought→IPV chain is assembled: the study explicitly could not test the proposed mediator. The two drought definitions have different analytical samples.
District hazard/risk examples are not assigned the national study's violence associations as local effect estimates. No armed-conflict pathway or reverse insecurity constraint was verified.

executive_assessment.text: Comparative district flood/drought and heat indices identify named differences; outdoor workers, people with limited shelter and other vulnerable groups face different coping constraints.

A national study finds drought–IPV associations, with different samples for precipitation and socioeconomic drought, but cannot establish causality or income mediation. Heat-plan counts describe planning coverage, not effectiveness.
